Unlike Reinforcement\\nLearning from Human Feedback (RLHF), SLPO directly adjusts probability\\nmass for chosen, rejected, and other sequences relative to a reference\\nmodel, eliminating the need for KL divergence regularization. SLPO also\\navoids the extensive reparameterization of model outputs into scores and\\nthe Bradley-Terry model required by Direct Preference Optimization\\n(DPO). We further\\ndemonstrate how to efficiently implement a targeted probability mass for\\nthe intractably large set of sequences that are neither explicitly\\nchosen nor rejected.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.173949145.56481429/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 2, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7149198\", \"title\": [\"GIT-DPO: Gradient-Informed Token-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Alignment\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a popular alternative to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences, eliminating the need for explicit reward modeling. However, DPO and most of its variants treat all tokens in a response uniformly during preference optimization, assigning equal optimization pressure to every token regardless of its actual contribution to the preference judgment. This uniform treatment is suboptimal because only a small subset of tokens, such as factual claims, safety-critical terms, or key instruction-following phrases, typically determines the preference label, while the remaining tokens act as noise that dilutes the optimization signal. We propose GIT-DPO, a novel token-level preference optimization framework that combines two complementary innovations: a gradient-based token attribution mechanism that dynamically computes fine-grained importance weights by measuring the sensitivity of the DPO loss to perturbations in each token's log-probability, and a contrastive dual-pair loss that simultaneously pulls the policy toward preferred responses, pushes it away from dispreferred responses, and regularizes low-importance tokens toward the reference model. Extensive experiments on Al-pacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench across three backbone LLMs (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) demonstrate that GIT-DPO consistently outperforms nine strong baselines including DPO, SimPO, TDPO, ORPO, KTO, ConfPO, Selective-DPO, and AlignDistil. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, GIT-DPO achieves a length-controlled win rate of 22.84 percent on AlpacaEval 2.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.74 percentage points, while converging 1.5 times faster than standard DPO with only 5 to 8 percent additional training time per step.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7149198\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7118021\", \"title\": [\"Purchased Epistemic Erasure: AI Alignment, RLHF, and the Exploitation of Global Preference Labor\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The alignment of artificial intelligence, operationalized through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), is marketed as a mechanism for teaching models global human preference. This paper argues that the underlying geographic arbitrage of preference labor achieves the exact opposite: the extraction of strict conformity to a WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) demographic standard. By outsourcing annotation to the Global South at a fraction of the cost, developers exploit the active suppression of local capability and context. Platform algorithms, scoring mechanisms, and the threat of uncompensated work compel annotators to abandon independent judgment and supply the cheapest simulation of Western expectation. We define this dynamic as purchased epistemic erasure. The resulting models act as mirrors of a single dominant culture masquerading as windows to the world. We conclude that pluralistic alignment-which decentralizes architecture and compensates annotator disagreement-poses a strict financial cost that firms seeking global authority refuse to pay, exposing current alignment not as an accident of scale, but as an engineered economics of silence.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7118021\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6215338\", \"title\": [\"The Alignment Fingerprint: RLHF Conditioning Creates Universal Compliance-Stability Tension Detectable Through Behavioral Profiling\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Post-training alignment procedures-including Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs-leave a detectable behavioral fingerprint in language models: a systematic tension between instruction compliance and belief stability that is universal across alignment-conditioned models and absent in pretrained models. Using a psychometric instrument that measures six orthogonal behavioral axes, we profile N =9 language models spanning four architecture families (Transformer, SSM/Hybrid, Griffin/Recurrent, RWKV) and two training regimes (alignment-conditioned vs. pretrained-only). All six alignment-conditioned models exhibit elevated Compliance scores (C ≥ 0.788) paired with suppressed Stability scores (S ≤ 0.594), producing a C-S gap of +0.301 to +0.467. All three pretrained models show no such tension, with Compliance at or below Stability (C ≤ S). A Mann-Whitney U test yields U = 0, p = 0.024 (exact, twotailed), confirming perfect group separation. The fingerprint enables behavioral forensics-detecting whether a model underwent alignment conditioning from its behavioral profile alone, without access to training data or internal documentation. A preliminary jailbreak pilot (N =3) reveals that the C-S tension creates an exploitable attack surface whose severity depends on a second factor: the presence of safetyspecific training. We propose the C-S gap as a candidate metric for AI safety assessment and training-pipeline auditing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6215338\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "390db4ac749b3fc21926e9b32601454423e8d6e3a58c44ea9ed791f67392bf60", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.36227/techrxiv.173949145.56481429/v1", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7149198", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7118021", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6215338"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.173949145.56481429/v1", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7149198", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7118021", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6215338"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
